Recruiting fintech talent starts with sourcing from fintech-specific communities and conferences, screening for hybrid finance-plus-technology skills, and offering pay near the $123K U.S. fintech average. Global fintech investment reached $103.1 billion across 2,100 deals in the first half of 2026 alone, according to [KPMG's Pulse of Fintech H1 2026](https://kpmg.com/xx/en/what-we-do/industries/financial-services/pulse-of-fintech.html). Six months earlier, the figure was $72.2 billion. Behind the resulting hiring race sits a finance talent squeeze, where only 15% of CFOs say their organizations aren't short on finance talent ([Deloitte 1Q 2025 CFO Signals Survey](https://www.deloitte.com/us/en/insights/topics/business-strategy-growth/1q-2025-cfo-signals-survey.html)).

This guide covers exactly where fintech professionals gather, what they earn by role, which skills to screen for, and how to close candidates who have multiple competing offers. You'll also get sourcing strategies for the hardest-to-fill roles - from blockchain developers commanding $200K+ to compliance engineers who understand both RegTech and AML law.

> **TL;DR:**
>

> - **The hybrid skills paradox is the core problem.** Professionals need finance domain knowledge plus technical chops: PCI-DSS on top of Python, AML law on top of AI model evaluation. Qualified crossover talent is scarce.

## Why Is Fintech Talent So Hard to Hire?

Finance and accounting roles take 35 to 60 days to fill, according to [The Resource Company's 2025 time-to-fill benchmarks](https://www.theresource.com/2025/10/27/time-to-fill-by-industry/). Fintech positions often take even longer because candidates need a rare mix of skills that doesn't fit neatly into "tech" or "finance" buckets.

Recruiters call this the hybrid skills paradox. A machine learning engineer at a payments company doesn't just need Python and TensorFlow - they also need to understand PCI-DSS compliance, transaction fraud patterns, and financial reporting standards. A compliance analyst at a neobank isn't just tracking regulations - they're evaluating AI model outputs for fairness and bias. These crossover skill sets shrink the qualified talent pool dramatically.

Why does this matter right now? Because the financial technology sector is growing roughly 3x faster than traditional banking, according to [McKinsey](https://www.mckinsey.com/industries/financial-services/our-insights/fintechs-a-new-paradigm-of-growth). Global investment in the sector reached $116 billion across 4,719 deals in 2025 ([KPMG](https://kpmg.com/xx/en/media/press-releases/2026/02/global-fintech-investment-rebounds-in-2025-supported-by-stronger-exit-activity.html)). Much of that capital is translating directly into headcount growth - and every new hire competes for the same small pool of candidates who can bridge the technology-finance divide.

According to [SHRM's 2025 Talent Trends report](https://www.shrm.org/topics-tools/research/2025-talent-trends/recruiting) (surveying 2,040 HR professionals), 69% of organizations report difficulty recruiting for full-time positions. Within fintech specifically, recruiters face three compounding pressures:

**Big Tech competition for the same engineers.** Google, Amazon, Meta, and Apple recruit the same software developers and data scientists that fintech startups need. These companies often match or exceed fintech pay - without the startup risk. [BLS](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/computer-and-information-technology/software-developers.htm) projects employment of software developers, QA analysts, and testers to grow 10% from 2025 to 2035. Software developers earned a median $135,980 in May 2025, and demand across every tech sector keeps intensifying.

**Salary compression drives passive candidate interest.** [Selby Jennings' 2025 fintech compensation survey](https://www.selbyjennings.com/en-us/industry-insights/hiring-advice/rebuilding-fintech-teams-in-2025-compensation-culture-and-competition-for-talent) found that 51% of fintech professionals received a raise, yet nearly half of those raises were worth only 1-5%. Small internal raises are what push employed people to listen. That gap means passive fintech talent is quietly open to outreach - if you know how to reach them.

**Equity is expected, not differentiating.** In [Ledgy's State of Equity 2025 report](https://ledgy.com/blog/equity-compensation-strategies-in-2025/), 82% of respondents said they own equity in their company. Stock options used to close borderline candidates. Today, in startup-heavy sectors like fintech, they're table stakes. You need something beyond equity to stand out.

**Pin's take:** Recruiters using Pin report a consistent pattern in fintech hiring: the professionals who close fastest aren't always labeled "fintech." Banking engineers, govtech product managers, and healthcare compliance professionals already speak the regulatory language that pure tech hires take months to absorb. When sourcing, search for skill combinations rather than industry labels. A Python engineer with SOC 2 audit experience is a stronger fintech hire than someone whose only signal is an industry label. Those crossover profiles see fewer competing offers. That matters a lot when the labeled talent pool is small and every recruiter is already working it. Pin's multi-source database, spanning 850M+ profiles across GitHub, Stack Overflow, patents, and professional networks, surfaces this undercontacted layer. Recruiters who shift from industry-filter sourcing to skills-combination sourcing consistently report higher candidate acceptance rates and shorter time-to-fill, because the pool is larger and fewer recruiters compete for each individual.

## What Does Fintech Talent Actually Earn?

Average fintech salaries sit at $123,495, ranging from $88,000 to $151,000, with 90th-percentile earners above $184,500, according to the [Georgia Fintech Academy's 2025 Salary Guide](https://georgiafintechacademy.org/fintech-salary-guide-2025-complete-compensation-overview/). That average masks huge variation by role. Specialized AI, blockchain, and security positions can exceed $200,000 in base salary alone.

Second, geographic arbitrage is real: sourcing from Atlanta or Austin for a remote-friendly position saves 15-20% on pay compared to Bay Area hires, without sacrificing talent quality.

## Which Skills Are in Highest Demand for Financial Technology Roles?

Six skill categories are in highest demand across financial technology companies: AI/ML, blockchain, cloud security, data engineering, payments infrastructure, and RegTech - all requiring domain expertise that takes years to build. [BLS](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/math/data-scientists.htm) projects data scientist employment to grow 34.6% from 2025 to 2035, roughly 10x the 3.5% average for all occupations. Information security analysts follow at 21% projected growth. Both figures represent baseline demand across all industries, but the financial technology sector amplifies them because positions require these skills combined with financial domain expertise.

Here's where the hiring gets specific. The skills recruiters should screen for fall into six categories, and the strongest candidates will have depth in at least two:

**AI and machine learning.** TensorFlow, PyTorch, and large language model fine-tuning. Applications in the sector include fraud detection, credit scoring, algorithmic trading, and personalized financial advice. AI-focused fintech deals drew $21.4 billion across 800 deals in the first half of 2026, nearly matching the $23.6 billion invested in all of 2025, per [KPMG](https://kpmg.com/xx/en/what-we-do/industries/financial-services/pulse-of-fintech.html). Teams are hiring aggressively for these profiles. See our roundup of [AI sourcing tools](/blog/best-ai-sourcing-tools-2026/) for platforms purpose-built to identify this talent.

**Blockchain and digital assets.** Solidity, Rust (for Solana), and smart contract auditing. Digital assets investment reached $21.9 billion across 1,335 deals in 2025 ([KPMG](https://kpmg.com/xx/en/what-we-do/industries/financial-services/pulse-of-fintech.html)). Deeper blockchain sourcing context appears in our guide to [recruiting blockchain developers](https://www.pin.com/blog/recruiting-blockchain-talent/).

**Cloud security and DevSecOps.** AWS, Azure, and GCP security configurations, combined with SOC 2 compliance experience. Financial data handling requires encryption at rest and in transit, strict access controls, and audit logging - making security engineers with payments or banking experience especially valuable.

**Data engineering.** Spark, dbt, SQL, and real-time streaming architectures. Every company in this sector drowns in transaction data. The ones that win build data pipelines that transform that data into credit decisions, fraud alerts, and customer insights in milliseconds.

**Payments infrastructure.** API integrations, PCI-DSS compliance, ACH/wire processing, and card network protocols. This is the plumbing of financial technology, and experienced payments engineers are scarce because the domain knowledge takes years to build.

**RegTech and compliance engineering.** AML (Anti-Money Laundering), KYC (Know Your Customer), and automating regulatory reporting. [Deloitte's Future Finance Trends 2025 report](https://www.deloitte.com/us/en/what-we-do/capabilities/finance-transformation/articles/future-finance-trends-2025.html) found that 64% of finance leaders plan to add more technical skills to their finance teams in 2025 and 2026. AML/KYC role postings rose 98% year-over-year according to [Ravio's 2025 Fintech Compensation Trends report](https://ravio.com/blog/fintech-compensation-trends) - a signal that compliance roles are becoming increasingly technical and increasingly difficult to fill.

## Where Do Fintech Professionals Actually Spend Their Time?

The five highest-signal sourcing channels for fintech professionals are industry conferences (Money20/20, Fintech Meetup), Slack communities (This Week in Fintech), niche networks (PaymentGenes), GitHub for engineering roles, and AI sourcing platforms that search across multiple data sources simultaneously. Traditional job boards underperform because fintech talent clusters in these specialized communities instead.

### Fintech-Specific Conferences

**Money20/20** draws 10,000+ attendees to its U.S. show and is the largest financial technology event globally. Payments executives, product leaders, and senior engineers attend. It's expensive but high-signal - attendees are employed, senior, and deeply embedded in the ecosystem.

**Fintech Meetup** (5,000+ attendees) uses a meeting-matching system that generates over 50,000 scheduled one-on-one conversations. For recruiters, this format is ideal - you can pre-schedule meetings with candidates rather than working a booth.

**FinovateFall** attracts 2,000+ senior decision-makers, and roughly 70% of them are senior leaders (C-suite, SVPs, founders, and department heads). Executive and senior leadership professionals for fintech concentrate here more than at any other industry event.

### Online Communities and Slack Groups

**This Week in Fintech (TWIF) Slack** gathers operators, founders, and investors across the sector. The premium tier is especially valuable for sourcing - members are active practitioners, not job seekers, which makes outreach feel less transactional.

**PaymentGenes** is a payments-specific talent network that hosts events and maintains a community of payments professionals across Europe and the U.S. It's niche, but if you're filling payments engineering or product roles, the signal-to-noise ratio is high.

### Technical Platforms

Engineering roles start with GitHub, the gold standard for passive sourcing. Search for contributors to open-source fintech projects - payment processing libraries, blockchain frameworks, and compliance automation tools. Professionals with active commit histories on fintech-adjacent repos are far more qualified than those who simply list "fintech" on their LinkedIn profile.

Pin's AI scans 850M+ profiles to identify candidates with the right mix of technical and financial domain skills - [**source financial technology talent with Pin**](https://www.pin.com/).

### Fintech Hiring Hubs by City

Location matters for sourcing strategy, even for remote roles. The strongest fintech talent pools concentrate in a handful of cities:

-   **San Francisco Bay Area** - The deepest fintech engineering pool, and the most expensive, at 20-30% above national pay averages.
-   **New York City** - Particularly strong for payments, trading technology, and RegTech talent, at 15-25% above national pay.
-   **London** - Europe's fintech capital. Strong in open banking and embedded finance.
-   **Singapore** - Asia-Pacific's fintech hub. Government-backed regulatory sandboxes attract compliance-savvy engineers.
-   **Austin and Atlanta** - Emerging hubs with 5-10% (Austin) and 5-15% (Atlanta) salary premiums, vs. 20-30% in SF. Growing rapidly as companies decentralize from traditional hubs.

Broader technical sourcing strategy - spanning multiple channels beyond fintech-specific ones - appears in our [guide to sourcing strategies for tech recruiting](https://www.pin.com/blog/tech-recruitment-sourcing-strategies/).

## How to Recruit Fintech Specialists in the U.S. Market

Recruiting fintech specialists in the U.S. market means planning for three things general tech hiring rarely touches: securities registration, state pay-transparency laws, and talent that clusters in a few metros. Sort them out before the first outreach message and you avoid the late-stage surprises that stall offers.

**Build licensing into the timeline.** Roles at broker-dealers and investment platforms often require FINRA registration. A candidate must hold the [Series 7 before sitting for the Series 24](https://www.finra.org/registration-exams-ce/individuals) principal exam, and the hiring firm files the Form U4. Under [FINRA Rule 1010](https://www.finra.org/rules-guidance/rulebooks/finra-rules/1010), fingerprints must follow promptly, or the registration goes inactive and the person can't do registered business. Ask about current registrations in the first screen.

**Post pay ranges where the law requires them.** California, Colorado, New York, and Washington all require salary ranges in job postings, and those states hold a large share of U.S. fintech employers. A competitive, published band also filters out candidates you can't afford.

**Source by metro, then widen.** Start in New York and the Bay Area for payments, trading, and RegTech roles, then widen to Atlanta and Austin, where pay premiums run 5-15% instead of 20-30%. Don't skip bank and insurer engineering teams in those same cities, since they are a proven feeder for fintech.

## How to Screen for Hybrid Finance-Tech Skills

Effective fintech screening requires testing for both technical depth and financial domain knowledge - the strongest hires demonstrate competence in at least two of six critical skill categories. Biggest screening mistake in fintech recruiting: treating it like standard tech hiring. A software engineer who built a social media app isn't automatically qualified to build a payments processing system that handles PCI-DSS compliance, reconciling transactions, and generating regulatory reports. Domain knowledge gaps drive most mis-hires.

Here's a screening framework that works across financial technology roles:

1.  **Map the role's regulatory exposure.** Before you write the job description, identify which financial regulations touch the role. A backend engineer working on a lending product needs to understand Fair Lending Act implications. A data engineer at a crypto exchange needs BSA/AML awareness. Build these into your screening questions - not as "do you know what GDPR is?" trivia, but as practical scenarios: "How would you design a data pipeline that satisfies both real-time fraud detection and SOX audit trail requirements?"
2.  **Test for financial domain translation.** Give candidates a business problem, not just a coding challenge. For example: "Our payment processing latency spikes during month-end settlement. Walk me through how you'd diagnose and fix it." This reveals whether someone can connect engineering choices to financial outcomes - the hallmark of a strong hire in this space.
3.  **Evaluate cross-functional communication.** Financial technology teams include engineers, compliance officers, product managers, and sometimes regulators. Candidates need to explain technical decisions in business terms and understand why compliance constraints exist. Ask them to describe a time they adjusted a technical approach because of a regulatory requirement.
4.  **Assess startup resilience (for early-stage companies).** Financial technology startups operate under regulatory scrutiny that most tech startups don't face. Candidates from Big Tech or traditional finance may not be prepared for the pace and ambiguity of a company that's simultaneously building product, applying for licenses, and responding to regulatory inquiries. Ask about their experience with ambiguity and shifting priorities.

Strongest hires in this sector come from three backgrounds. Traditional finance professionals who taught themselves to code, software engineers who spent 2+ years at a financial institution, and professionals from regulated industries (healthcare tech, govtech) who already understand compliance-driven development all make strong fintech hires.

Pin's data backs the bank-to-fintech path. In a sample of 13,000+ U.S. engineers at fintech companies founded since 2005, drawn from Pin's index, 14.5% have a bank or insurer in their documented career history. That is about 1.4x the rate for engineers at software companies outside finance (10.2%). Recruiters also report that professionals who spent 3-5 years at a bank or insurer before joining a startup tend to outperform pure startup hires. They've internalized the regulatory mindset that you can't teach in an onboarding week, and they're hungry for the speed and ownership that startups offer. When sourcing, don't overlook traditional financial services firms as a talent pipeline - their engineers already speak both languages.

## How to Close Fintech Candidates With Competing Offers

Senior candidates in this sector often field several competing offers at once. Bonuses, equity, and some remote flexibility are now baseline expectations, so a standard equity package and a hybrid policy won't differentiate your offer.

What actually closes candidates in this market:

**Speed.** A 35-to-60-day fill cycle for finance roles is a liability, not a benchmark. Pin users fill positions in an average of 14 days. Strong candidates holding multiple offers rarely wait out a six-week process.

**Pay transparency from the first conversation.** Don't wait until the final round to discuss money. Applicants in this sector know the ranges (they read the same salary guides you do). Share your band early. If it's competitive, the transparency builds trust; if not, you save everyone's time. Use [salary benchmarking tools](/blog/salary-benchmarking-tools/) to validate your bands before the first call.

**Mission clarity over generic perks.** Financial technology professionals chose this sector because they believe technology can improve financial services. "We're building the future of payments" resonates more than "we have unlimited PTO." Be specific about the problem you're solving, who benefits, and what the candidate's role looks like in six months.

**Remote flexibility is expected.** Roles that require five days in-office have already eliminated most of the talent pool before a single application arrives, because fintech professionals who hold competing offers will filter those positions out immediately.

As Rich Rosen, Executive Recruiter at Cornerstone Search, puts it: "Absolutely Money maker for Recruiters... in 6 months i can directly attribute over $250k in revenue to [Pin](https://www.pin.com/)." In a market where speed determines whether you close a hire or lose them to a competitor, AI-powered sourcing tools make the difference between a filled position and a three-month vacancy.

## Where Is Fintech Hiring Headed?

Fintech is on track to become a $1.5 trillion industry by 2030, roughly 6x its 2022 size, according to BCG and QED Investors. [McKinsey](https://www.mckinsey.com/industries/financial-services/our-insights/fintechs-a-new-paradigm-of-growth) estimates fintech revenues are growing roughly 3x faster than traditional banking. That growth trajectory means fintech hiring isn't slowing down - it's accelerating and shifting.

<figure style="margin:2rem 0;padding:0;line-height:0"><img src="data:image/svg+xml;base64," alt="Projected Job Growth for Fintech Roles (2024-2034)" style="width:100%;height:auto;display:block;border-radius:12px"></figure>

[World Economic Forum's Future of Jobs Report 2025](https://www.weforum.org/publications/the-future-of-jobs-report-2025/) identifies fintech engineers, big data, and AI/ML specialists as the fastest-growing positions globally. 86% of employers expect AI and information processing to transform their business by 2030. Three areas are seeing the most aggressive hiring right now:

**AI governance and model risk.** As fintechs deploy AI for credit decisions, fraud detection, and customer service, they need people who can audit those models for fairness, explainability, and regulatory compliance. These roles barely existed two years ago. Now they're some of the hardest to fill.

**Stablecoin and tokenization infrastructure.** Regulatory clarity in the U.S. through late 2025 unlocked a wave of institutional adoption. Companies building stablecoin payment rails, tokenized securities platforms, and digital asset custody solutions are hiring aggressively. Digital assets investment hit $11.1 billion across 467 deals in the first half of 2026, already above the full-year totals for 2023 and 2024 ([KPMG](https://kpmg.com/xx/en/what-we-do/industries/financial-services/pulse-of-fintech.html)).

**Payments infrastructure.** Payments investment jumped to $44.2 billion in the first half of 2026, led by a $24.3 billion acquisition of a large global payments company ([KPMG](https://kpmg.com/xx/en/what-we-do/industries/financial-services/pulse-of-fintech.html)). Consolidation like that creates integration work, and payments engineers who know card networks, ACH, and PCI-DSS are already scarce.

At the same time, certain segments are cooling. InsurTech investment fell to $3.7 billion in the first half of 2026 on its weakest deal volume since 2016, and wealthtech drew just $220 million across 32 deals ([KPMG](https://kpmg.com/xx/en/what-we-do/industries/financial-services/pulse-of-fintech.html)). Recruiters should watch where capital flows - it's the most reliable leading indicator of where fintech hiring will intensify over the next 6-12 months.

What does this mean for your sourcing strategy? Focus your pipeline building on the sectors where capital is flowing. Placing applicants in AI, payments, or digital assets means demand will likely outstrip supply for the next 12-18 months. In cooler segments like wealthtech and InsurTech, fewer companies are hiring, so expect fewer openings but less competition for the candidates you approach.

For related reading on how AI is reshaping technical recruiting more broadly, see our guide on [hiring for AI roles](https://www.pin.com/blog/hiring-ai-engineers/).

### How long does it take to hire fintech talent?

Finance and accounting roles typically take 35 to 60 days to fill, according to [The Resource Company](https://www.theresource.com/2025/10/27/time-to-fill-by-industry/) (2025). Recruiting fintech talent often takes longer due to multi-stage interviews, regulatory background checks such as FINRA fingerprinting, and competing offers. Companies using AI-powered sourcing and automated outreach tools reduce this timeline significantly - Pin users fill positions in an average of 14 days, the fastest time-to-fill of any AI recruiting platform.

### What skills should recruiters screen for in fintech candidates?

Screen for hybrid skills that combine technology and financial domain knowledge. The six critical skill categories are: AI/ML frameworks (TensorFlow, PyTorch), blockchain and smart contracts (Solidity, Rust), cloud security (AWS/Azure/GCP with SOC 2 experience), data engineering (Spark, dbt), payments infrastructure (PCI-DSS, ACH), and RegTech (AML/KYC compliance). The strongest candidates demonstrate depth in at least two categories.

### Is fintech hiring growing or shrinking?

BCG and QED Investors project fintech will reach $1.5 trillion in revenue by 2030. While some fintechs have cut customer-facing roles (Block eliminated roughly 4,000 positions in early 2026), engineering, AI, compliance, and security teams continue to expand. The [BLS](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/math/data-scientists.htm) projects 34.6% growth for data scientists and 21% for information security analysts from 2025 to 2035.

## Key Takeaways

-   Fintech talent requires hybrid skills that combine technology and financial domain knowledge - the shallow candidate pool is the #1 sourcing challenge
-   Average fintech salaries sit at $123K, with blockchain and AI specialists commanding $150K-$200K+. Geographic premiums add 15-30% in major hubs
-   Source from fintech-specific communities (Money20/20, This Week in Fintech, PaymentGenes), not just job boards and LinkedIn
-   Screen for regulatory awareness alongside technical skills - the ability to connect engineering decisions to compliance requirements separates good fintech hires from great ones
-   Speed matters: 35-to-60-day finance hiring cycles lose candidates who hold competing offers. AI sourcing tools compress the sourcing-to-offer cycle
-   Watch where capital flows - payments ($44.2B), AI ($21.4B), and digital assets ($11.1B) led H1 2026 fintech investment and are the hottest hiring sectors heading into 2027
